query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: Under service-relevant thermal aging and cyclic loading, a single-phase high-entropy alloy undergoes grain-boundary segregation of a segregation-prone minor element (such as Mn) that promotes the nucleation of brittle intergranular precipitates, thereby degrading its toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogenized, single-phase high-entropy alloy (e.g., CrMnFeCoNi) with a uniform elemental distribution and minimal pre-existing precipitates.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to elevated temperatures (e.g., around 700°C) for durations sufficient to drive atomic redistribution, combined with cyclic mechanical loading that simulates service conditions.
generation.conditions: Service-like conditions including thermal aging at high temperatures and cyclic loading; controlled comparison between a standard alloy containing a segregation-prone element (e.g., Mn) and a variant where that element is replaced or its segregation is inhibited.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries, where the accumulation of the minor element leads to nanoscale clustering and the formation of brittle intergranular precipitates (e.g., L10-NiMn or Cr-rich sigma phases).
generation.mechanism: The thermal and mechanical stresses promote diffusion of the susceptible element to the grain boundaries. This segregation at the interfaces facilitates nanoscale phase separation, forming brittle precipitates that decrease grain-boundary cohesion and overall toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: The alloy containing the segregation-prone element will exhibit a marked reduction in ductility and toughness relative to its modified counterpart, with microstructural analyses (via TEM or APT) revealing intergranular brittle precipitates. In contrast, the modified alloy with reduced segregation will better maintain its toughness under the same conditions.
generation.baseline: The initial, homogenized HEA exhibits high toughness and ductility with a uniform elemental distribution and no significant grain-boundary precipitates under ambient conditions.
generation.boundary: This embrittlement mechanism is expected to be prominent under prolonged high-temperature exposure and cyclic mechanical loading that mimic demanding engineering service conditions; effects may be minimal under low temperature or static conditions.
generation.uncertainty: Exact thresholds for temperature, loading duration, and the critical concentration of the segregating element required to trigger precipitate formation are not fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of initially single-phase HEA samples: one standard alloy containing the segregation-prone element, and a modified alloy where that element is either reduced or replaced by an element less prone to segregation. Subject both sets to identical service-like thermal aging (e.g., exposure at ~700°C for selected durations) combined with cyclic mechanical loading. Analyze the microstructure at grain boundaries using TEM and atom probe tomography (APT) and perform mechanical tests to assess toughness and ductility.
measurements: Grain-boundary composition and precipitate formation via APT
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both alloys exhibit similar mechanical behavior (no significant reduction in ductility or toughness) and no detectable formation of brittle intergranular precipitates under the tested conditions, then the hypothesis that grain-boundary segregation of the segregation-prone element drives embrittlement is falsified.

It has been shown that the residual strain generated by cold rolling can promote the diffusion of Cr into GBs during subsequent annealing processes, leading to the formation of Cr-rich σ phases in Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni system HEAs (, ). Therefore, it is reasonable to infer that plastic deformation can facilitate the segregation of elements Cr, Ni, and Mn into GBs in current HEA. However, the low-level concentration of these elements is insufficient for precipitating Cr-rich σ, body-centered cubic (bcc) Cr, or L10-NiMn phases (table S1) (, , ). In addition, the short exposure (10 min) at 700°C is insufficient to precipitate σ phase, as confirmed by TEM (Fig. 4A). cited_evidence.text: Segregation of minor alloying elements to GBs often embrittles conventional alloys (, ). Grain refinement is an effective way to evade GB embrittlement because more interfaces reduce the level of individual GB segregation (). In contrast, multiple principal constitutive elements in HEAs can segregate into GBs instead of trace alloying elements. In HEAs, grain refinement can assist the segregation of principal constitutive elements to GBs and even lead to the formation of brittle intermetallic phases at GBs (). For example, Cr-rich bcc phases and L10-NiMn phases precipitate at GBs in nanocrystalline Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEA (grain size, ~50 nm) after annealing at 450°C for only 5 min, which reduces the ductility substantially (). In addition, previous studies show that Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEAs with the grain sizes from 4.4 to 155 μm all exhibit loss of ductility at intermediate temperatures, irrespective of grain size in this range (Fig. 1). Microalloying with B in Fe-Mn steels has been reported to delay temper embrittlement at 450°C (). Although recent experimental measurements of HAGB energy with this same alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) exist, a comparison of this prediction is difficult. Measurements of grain boundary energy are sensitive to thermally-driven grain boundary segregation (and possibly phase separation) of impurities. This value is relatively high for metals,, and may imply a propensity for localized cohesive failure or fracture at the boundaries. Grain boundary decohesion has been recently shown to occur readily for this alloy due to segregation and nanoclustering of Cr, Ni and Mn at elevated temperature, and these failures typically originate along HAGBs and at triple junctions. In the present work there is no significant evidence of grain boundary segregation, and this is reasonable as a negligible increase in temperature is expected for these sliding conditions. This suggests that this alloy may also be prone to grain boundary decohesion without significant segregation and phase separation, i.e., when it is a solid solution.
